summary: For children aged 5–6 learning to name everyday materials (wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock, plus paper, fabric, brick, elastic). The teaching objective is to attach each material word to the substance shared by many different objects — not to a single item — through handling and naming real exemplars, active naming hunts, and deliberate work on the tricky cases (water and rock) and look-alike pairs (glass vs clear plastic; metal vs shiny grey plastic). Build spoken vocabulary; no reading required.
misconceptions: 'Material' means only cloth/fabric, so children fail to name glass, metal, water or rock as materials.
Water is not a material because it is a liquid, not a solid 'thing'.
Rock and stone are different materials, when 'stone' is just a word for smaller pieces of rock.
A material name is tied to one object (wood = 'a pencil') rather than to the substance shared by many objects.
All plastic is hard and all metal is silver, so children misname materials by a single expected appearance.

activities.title: Name the material: one word, many objects
steps: Handle and name a set of real objects, saying what each one is MADE of (e.g. a wooden door, a wooden spoon, a wooden ruler, wooden toy blocks).
Group objects that share a material together so the child sees the same word — 'wood' — belongs to several different objects.
Deliberately include a cup/puddle of water and a garden stone, naming water and rock aloud as materials.
Point to and name one object that is made of more than one material (e.g. a pencil with an eraser on top: wood, pencil 'lead' (graphite), paint, a metal band and a rubber eraser).
activities.insight: A material name refers to the substance something is made of, and one material word belongs to many different objects, whatever the object's shape or use.

activities.title: Material hunt with a tally
steps: Go on a naming hunt around the room: find as many things made of metal as you can in a set time, then do the same for wood, and so on. Give every material the same amount of time and don't set a fixed number.
Record each find in a simple frequency table, tallying how many objects of each material are found.
For an object made of more than one material, record it under each of its materials.
Look at the finished tally and say which materials you found most often in the place you searched.
activities.insight: Materials are all around us, and an open-ended hunt can show which materials turn up most often in a particular place; active, repeated naming in use is intended to make the vocabulary more secure than reciting a list alone.

activities.title: Water, rock and the look-alike test
steps: Confirm that water is a material: name the sea, a puddle and ice as all being the material water.
Confirm that rock is a material shared by many objects (a stone wall, a stone statue, a stone kerb, gravel), and that rock and stone are the same material.
Compare near-neighbour pairs — a glass jar and a clear plastic cup, and a metal object and a shiny grey plastic one — and decide which is which.

Name a metal object that is not shiny or not silver-coloured (e.g. a rusty iron nail, or a copper-coloured coin, which may be shiny but is not silver), and point out that not all plastic is hard — so a material cannot be judged by one expected look.

Use a quick check beyond looking: tap it, feel its weight and how cold it feels, and gently see if it bends (never try to bend glass) — and name the material by how it behaves, remembering this check is a helpful clue rather than a certain test.
activities.insight: A material is what something is made of in any state and wherever it comes from, so liquids and natural solids count; and material is judged by how it behaves and feels, not by appearance alone (clear is not always glass; shiny is not always metal; metal need not be shiny; plastic need not be hard).

checkQuestion: Lay out about eight things: a wooden block, a plastic toy, a glass jar, a metal key, a cup of water, a pebble, a sheet of paper, a woolly sock. Say: 'Tell me what each one is MADE of.' Then hold up the water and the pebble: 'Is water a material? Is a rock a material? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: Names wood, plastic, glass, metal, paper and fabric for the clear cases; recognises that WATER and ROCK are also materials — a material is what something is made of, whatever its state or where it comes from.
